stories.topic: Sara Rai: 'We Had Nothing Else to Do, So We Looked at Things'
stories.summary: While recording a Seen and the Unseen episode with the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand's granddaughter, Amit was struck by how precise and evocative her childhood memories were. They sounded like crafted fiction. He asked how she remembered so much. Her answer was that there was nothing else to do, so they looked at things. Amit links this to growing up in the 70s and 80s: books, music and films were scarce, but time was plentiful, and he daydreamed a great deal.
stories.insight: Deep observation and rich memory grow out of unfilled time. When the scroll-and-swipe treadmill fills every gap, the attention that once went to the world around us gets spent elsewhere, and paying close attention becomes something we have to choose deliberately.
stories.quote: And I said, Sara how do you remember so much? And she was like, we had nothing else to do. So we looked at things.

stories.topic: The Mixtapes Made for a Future Wife
stories.summary: Amit pulls out a TDK and a Sony cassette. He made these mixtapes at nineteen for the seventeen-year-old girl he was wooing, whom he later married. Making one was hard work. Foreign music was hard to find. You recorded in real time on a double-deck player, coordinated the two tapes, and worked out how many minutes of songs would fit on each side. He says that with the people he was wooing, mixtapes had a hundred percent strike rate.
stories.insight: A gift that costs real time and effort says 'this is who I am, and I want you to like it' in a way that a one-minute Spotify playlist can't. Choosing what to include also forces you to work out what you love and why, so making the tape shapes the maker as well as the receiver.
stories.quote: when you sit down and you curate the music you love and you want to share, you are in a sense also curating yourself.

stories.topic: Posting Letters to a Classmate Two Buildings Away
stories.summary: In Class 8, Ajay and his friend Manisha Purohit sat one desk apart at school and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East. They still began a ritual of writing letters to each other: writing at home, dropping the letter in a post box, and waiting for a physical reply.
stories.insight: Letters were worth writing even when you saw the person every day, because the form itself asks for care. You write carefully and you read carefully, and that is a different kind of exchange from conversation.
stories.quote: Just you're living two buildings away. But it's a delight to write and get those physical pieces of paper

stories.topic: How CMIE Was Born from a Stack of Inland Letters
stories.summary: On 13 April 1976, Ajay's father came home and said he had been sacked. Asked what he would do, he said he would start a new organisation called CMIE. That same evening he wrote a pile of inland letters to friends all over India. Each explained what had happened, described the new venture, and asked for specific help.
stories.insight: A major institution was started with an evening of handwritten requests to a trusted network. Each letter carried a story and a specific ask. Ajay's lesson for today is that email can carry the same care and seriousness if we choose to write it that way.
stories.quote: And that's how like CMIE got started with handwritten inland letters sent out to friends all over the country saying, Help me, I'm trying to do this.

stories.topic: The Locked Godrej Almirah and Dad's 1967 Playboys
stories.summary: Every Godrej steel almirah in Amit's childhood home was left unlocked except the one in his father's study. Young Amit found the hidden key. Among video cassettes and books inside were stacks of Playboy and Mayfair. He shows two issues, May and November 1967, from when his father was about twenty-five or twenty-six. He reflects on how little information men of that era had about sex: there was no Debonair yet, Bollywood offered warped ideas of romance, and there was no internet. Then he turns the old joke around. He really did read Playboy for the stories. A Playboy fiction anthology he bought around 1998 or 1999 is where he first read Haruki Murakami ('The Second Bakery Attack'), alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov. In the 1980s, he says, the two prestigious places to publish a short story were The New Yorker and Playboy.
stories.insight: Scarcity changes the imaginative life. One locked cupboard held enormous value when there was nothing else available. The story also shows that serious literature and erotica shared the same pages: Playboy was a home for great fiction and long-form journalism.
stories.quote: there's this old saying where people will joke, I read Playboy for the stories. No, the thing is I actually did, because Playboy had a great tradition of publishing great short stories by the world's best writers.

stories.summary: Amit's father, a government servant, received stacks of official diaries every year. Knowing his son wanted to be a writer, he would hand them over and say 'Beta, likho' (son, write). In the 1986 diary, twelve-year-old Amit began a novel called 'Tales of Saint Johns'. Part one, chapter one was titled 'Tantalising Tantrums', which at least alliterates. He wrote a couple of chapters in handwriting far neater than today's, then stopped. The rest of the diary is empty.
stories.insight: For Amit the empty diary stands for all the writing he never did. It also points to a hidden privilege. Getting good at writing takes volume, enough pages that you can afford to throw some away, and many children never have that much paper.
stories.quote: So I think of this as an empty diary, which is, you know, my lament for all the writing that I haven't done

stories.topic: A Mother's Last Gift: Handwritten Recipes
stories.summary: Amit's mother died of pancreatic cancer in 2008. Knowing she was dying, she carefully wrote down recipes for all the dishes he loved, including a liver dish that is a particular favourite, and gave them to him. When he cleared out his late father's house, he also found a recipe book his maternal grandmother had written in the 1960s. It is in beautiful English and mixes Western and Indian recipes.
stories.insight: Handwritten recipes record how people lived inside. For a woman of his grandmother's generation, limited in many ways by her circumstances, cooking and collecting recipes was probably a rich part of her inner world rather than mere drudgery. Free YouTube recipes can't hold that kind of meaning.
stories.quote: She knew she was going to go. So before she went, she painstakingly wrote down recipes of all the stuff I liked and gave it to me.

stories.topic: A Recipe Book Compiled by Code
stories.summary: As a PhD student who had to cook, Ajay and Susan invented a fixed text-file format for writing down recipes. They wrote an AWK program that converted those files into LaTeX, which produced a PDF that became their recipe book. Amit's response was a mock 'sashtang pranam' (a full bow).
stories.insight: The same urge that drove handwritten family recipe books lives on in a programmer's household. The tools have changed, but the habit of keeping a personal, organised record of what you cook has not.
stories.quote: So there was a text file which represented a recipe in a fixed way, and there was an AWK program which translated that into uh LaTeX.

stories.topic: 'Creative Animal' and 'Manic Beast': Amit's MTV Visiting Cards
stories.summary: Amit was never the corporate or networking type. At MTV, his third job, they insisted he have a visiting card and asked for his designation. 'Writer' seemed too boring, so he asked for 'Creative Animal' and got it. Years later, after a promotion, they offered him something like 'senior supervising whatever'. He asked what a promotion from Creative Animal would be, and his new card said 'Manic Beast'.
stories.insight: Even a dull corporate formality can be a chance to be yourself. Refusing the template costs nothing and says something about who you are.
stories.quote: So I said, What is a promotion from creative animal? So I got Manic Beast.

stories.topic: Narendra Shenoy's Half-Hour on Michael Porter
stories.summary: Amit retells a story his friend Narendra Shenoy told on The Seen and the Unseen. Narendra had an arranged marriage with Sheila. Her twin sister had been matched with a smooth conversationalist, and Narendra was not one. Sheila once asked him whether he had anything to talk about. When he later called her long-distance while studying for an MBA in another city, he felt pressure to be interesting, so he spent half an hour explaining Michael Porter's business philosophy.
stories.insight: When a call was rare and expensive, it felt like a performance with a script you had to fill. Young men often had no idea what to say, and this is a gentle, funny example of that.
stories.quote: So for half an hour he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter.

stories.topic: The Badminton Partner Who Needed an 'Urgent' Phone Call
stories.summary: Amit came to Fergusson College's junior college straight from a boys' school and couldn't read signals from girls. A girl he played badminton with turned up at his house one day with a friend and asked to use his phone for an urgent call. She made the call and left. It took Amit years to realise this was probably a sign of interest, since nobody walks into a random person's house just to use the phone.
stories.insight: Before mobiles, the household landline could be an excuse for courtship. People missed the signals as easily then as they do now.
stories.quote: And it took me many years to kind of figure out that this was some kind of expression of interest in some way, because why the hell would you go into a random person house?

stories.summary: Ajay recalls a woman from Calcutta describing the city's barely working phone system. Sometimes you got no dial tone, and sometimes you picked up the receiver and heard someone else's conversation. Once she picked up the phone, found herself connected into a call between two strangers, and realised they were talking about her.
stories.insight: It's a reminder of how badly basic infrastructure used to work, and of how a broken system could produce a moment stranger than fiction.
stories.quote: it was wired together into some two people having a conversation, and it turned out that they were talking about her.

stories.topic: One Payphone for an Entire IIT Hostel
stories.summary: At IIT Bombay, Ajay's whole hostel shared one coin payphone, with a queue to make outgoing calls. For incoming calls, the watchman answered, heard something like 'I want to speak with Ajay Shah of 262', and shouted the room number across the hostel until the person ran down to take the call. Ajay also recalls that payphones in New York or Singapore were later turned into Wi-Fi points before every phone had internet.
stories.insight: Receiving a phone call used to be a public event. Shared infrastructure had its own social rituals, and those disappeared along with the device.
stories.quote: the watchman would come shouting two six two and then you would run down and pick up the phone.

stories.topic: The Three-Metre Map of India on the Family Wall
stories.summary: Ajay's father bought the four-sheet map of India sold by the Survey of India, built a wooden board of the right size, and pasted the sheets into a map about three metres by three metres that covered a wall of their home. Whenever a place or river came up, the children would scamper up to the map to find it. Ajay has tried for years to build a wall-sized map of the Himalayas and hasn't managed it. He believes a German company makes a good six-sheet set, and he asks listeners for leads.
stories.insight: A huge paper map on the wall makes geography part of everyday family life, something everyone looks at together. That is hard to recreate with a phone, and surprisingly hard to buy today.
stories.quote: And then it was just like standard operating procedure for us that any place names would appear, a river would appear, and like little kids would scamper up to the map and look at things

recommendations.item: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Brought up at the start, when Amit recalls how vividly Sara Rai described her childhood.
recommendations.reason: Her strikingly detailed memories, and her explanation that 'we had nothing else to do, so we looked at things', inspired the episode's argument that unfilled time sharpened attention.

recommendations.item: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (Episode 288 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing letters. Amit describes his novelist friend Chandrahas as someone who still writes emails like old-fashioned letters.
recommendations.reason: A living example that email can still carry long, narrative, memory-filled letters if the writer takes the trouble.

recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of letters becoming literature: Nehru's letters to his daughter added up to a book.
recommendations.reason: Ajay ranks it among the great intellectual creations, proof of what careful, sustained letter-writing can produce.

recommendations.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
recommendations.context: Paired with Nehru's book. Ajay says Tolkien's letters to his kids turned into The Hobbit.
recommendations.reason: Another case of a person writing to family and ending up with a book the world treasures.

recommendations.item: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
recommendations.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
recommendations.context: One of Amit's treasured books, bought around 1998–99, mentioned while showing his father's 1967 Playboys.
recommendations.reason: Evidence that Playboy published the world's best short-story writers. It's where Amit first read Murakami, alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov.

recommendations.creator: Haruki Murakami
recommendations.context: A short story that first appeared in Playboy and was Amit's first encounter with Murakami.
recommendations.reason: The example Amit names of the high-quality fiction Playboy carried.

recommendations.creator: Playboy (interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin)
recommendations.context: Ajay's interjection during the Playboy segment, reminding Amit that a Larry Page and Sergey Brin interview appeared in the magazine.
recommendations.reason: Shows that Playboy ran serious long-form journalism alongside its fiction.

recommendations.item: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
recommendations.creator: Robin Dunbar
recommendations.context: Mentioned while Amit explains Dunbar's number using an old address book.
recommendations.reason: The source of the idea that our brains can keep track of about 150 people, with around five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty.

recommendations.creator: Wah Chef
recommendations.context: Amit's favourite YouTube cooking video, mentioned while contrasting handwritten family recipe books with today's endless online recipes.
recommendations.reason: His personal favourite in the flood of online cooking videos.

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode where Narendra told the Michael Porter phone-call story that Amit retells in the STD booth segment.
recommendations.reason: Where to hear the full, charming arranged-marriage story and the rest of the conversation.

recommendations.item: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: Ajay calls it a great newspaper column on how mobile roaming wiped out the STD booth industry.
recommendations.reason: A clear real-world case of creative destruction: an industry employing millions disappeared, and India's dynamic market economy absorbed the people.

recommendations.item: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit points back to it during Ajay's lament about paper maps.
recommendations.reason: The hosts' earlier, fuller discussion of maps.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Borges when Ajay complains he can't find a good wall map of the Himalayas.
recommendations.reason: Borges's point that a perfectly accurate map would have to be as big as the territory, which Amit uses as a quip about Ajay's search.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the segment on answering machines.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ahead of the Beatles. It's where the song Answering Machine comes from.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Brought up after Ajay mentions answering machines.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great song with an immortal line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', whose sadness is lost on people who never used one.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay's case for cash draws on what Vitalik Buterin told the two hosts in Madras.
recommendations.reason: The conversation behind Ajay's argument that cash's universal acceptance and anonymity protect us from a surveillance society.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit describes the course while making the case for journaling. Students are given a subject and asked to journal daily.
recommendations.reason: It puts writing-as-self-discovery into practice. The journals must stay completely private, so students can think without a filter.

recommendations.item: The tweet that inspired this episode
recommendations.creator: @NoContextHumans
recommendations.context: Amit opens by citing a tweet asking what has quietly disappeared over the last twenty years without anyone noticing.
recommendations.reason: The question that set off the whole episode about lost objects.

recommendations.creator: Neil Young
recommendations.context: Listed among the resources in the show notes. It isn't discussed on air.
recommendations.reason: Included in the episode's show notes. The hosts don't say why on air.

core_ideas.concept: We Shape Our Objects, Then Our Objects Shape Us
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing for the episode. An object's importance goes beyond its function, because a whole culture of habits and rituals grows around it. When the object disappears, that world goes with it. So the point isn't nostalgia. It's to notice what those habits did to us.
core_ideas.quote: We shape our objects and then our objects shape us in ways that go far beyond the simple functionality.

core_ideas.concept: The Last Time You Did X
core_ideas.explanation: Objects drop out of our lives one at a time, and we rarely notice the moment it happens. Ajay suggests trying to be aware, as it happens, that you may be using something for the last time.
core_ideas.quote: Imagine if you could recall with each of these objects that this is the last time I did X.

core_ideas.explanation: In the 70s and 80s, books, music and films were scarce, but time was not. That spare time went into daydreaming and close observation. Today, constant scrolling and swiping leave little room for either, and Amit says this is a lament about himself, not a complaint about young people. Deep attention now takes deliberate effort.
core_ideas.quote: Because the one scarcity that was not so acute as today was time. We had a lot of time.

core_ideas.explanation: Mixtapes, handwritten letters and trips to the post office took hours, and that cost told the receiver you cared. Ajay argues that tasks demanding focus put the mind's full power to work and created beauty. An endless supply of frictionless content makes that level of focus harder to reach.
core_ideas.quote: we harnessed the CPU seconds of the mind into doing this and that created beauty

core_ideas.explanation: Amit, citing Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', argues that writing doesn't just express what you already think. It helps you discover yourself and produces new ideas, which is why he urges private daily journaling. Handwriting goes further, because it is slower, physical, and hard to edit. Ajay adds that this raises the level of thought that goes into it, and Amit wonders whether today's leaders, who no longer write long letters the way Nehru and Patel did, are lesser for it.
core_ideas.quote: when you write, you're not only expressing yourself, you are shaping yourself.

core_ideas.explanation: The tool doesn't force short, careless writing; we choose it. Ajay points out that Gmail keeps drafts, so you can edit one email for days until it's an essay. He and Lant Pritchett exchange 3,000-word emails that can take a month to answer, as a conversation meant to last years. Putting 'long form' in the subject line tells the reader this isn't an everyday email.
core_ideas.quote: You can edit it for days and you can make it a great essay. And only then you punch send.

core_ideas.explanation: Dunbar's number says our brains evolved to track about 150 people, roughly a tribe, with about five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty. The old household address book held all of them, plus the grocer, electrician and plumber, in one physical place. Every time you opened it, you were reminded who was in your life. Without that reminder, friendships fade unless we tend them on purpose.
core_ideas.quote: This is a physical manifestation of all the people you know in the world with their phone numbers.

core_ideas.concept: One-Way Journeys and Religion as a Mirror of Its Times
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay shares a friend's idea. For most of history, when someone left, you didn't know whether they would arrive safely or ever return. Video calls and safe air travel have ended that. Amit adds that religious rules often reflect the conditions of their time. The old Hindu ban on overseas travel can be read as elders' fear of losing the young for good, and the pork taboo as protection against disease.
core_ideas.quote: And one way to read it is that the elders were terrified that somebody young would go overseas and they would never come back.

core_ideas.explanation: You only get good at writing through volume, enough iterations that you can throw pages away. Many families could afford only the school notebooks they had to buy, so simply having paper to write in was a privilege. Scarcity has two effects. A child given his only diary will value every page, but that same scarcity can paralyse, letting perfection become the enemy of production.
core_ideas.quote: And it's actually a sign of great privilege.

core_ideas.concept: Asynchronous Messaging Is a New Mode of Being
core_ideas.explanation: Communication used to be either nothing or synchronous, like a planned call from an STD booth that had to be worth the trip. Now messages are asynchronous and always possible, so contact feels less urgent and often becomes trivial. Ajay's example is the 'did you take your meds today' message. It's a different frame of mind, not just a faster version of the old one.
core_ideas.quote: asynchronous messaging is a very different frame of mind compared to either nothing or synchronous.

core_ideas.concept: Creative Destruction: Job Loss Usually Isn't the Catastrophe It Seems
core_ideas.explanation: When mobile roaming arrived, more than a million STD booths employing millions of people vanished almost overnight. Ajay argues that in India's dynamic market economy, people move on to other jobs, so the gloom about technology destroying jobs is mostly misplaced.
core_ideas.quote: Most of the time in India, job loss is not a problem because there is a creative dynamic market economy and people move on, they get other jobs

core_ideas.concept: Paper Maps Give a Strategic View
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that well-made paper maps, like old Bartholomew or National Geographic maps, show the world in ways designed for a wall, giving a big-picture sense that Google Maps doesn't. He has even tried putting Google Maps on a large screen, but its labelling isn't designed for that. Children today can neither read nor fold a paper map.
core_ideas.quote: I think that there is a strategic sense that you see in a paper map that you don't see on Google Maps.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that cash's universal acceptance and anonymity are underrated, and that we only notice them once they're gone. In places like China, where the infrastructure for accepting cash has broken down, every transaction can be traced and you live in a panopticon. He calls using cash a social responsibility, drawing on what Vitalik Buterin told the hosts in Madras.
core_ideas.quote: Gentle reader, use cash more. It's your social responsibility to use cash more.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's practical tip: instead of a paper card, share a QR code linking to your contact file (a VCF). Google Contacts checks that link periodically, so any change to your details updates automatically in everyone's address book.
core_ideas.quote: In the modern world, you're supposed to have a QR of the URL of your VCF file.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay arrives hoarse and asks why Amit has a bag. Amit replies: 'I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes.'
Amit on mixtapes as a wooing device: 'as far as people you are wooing is concerned, hundred percent strike rate.'
Amit proposes a new Everything is Everything newsletter in which the two hosts write each other long letters. Ajay declines: 'But we talk too much. You also need a little starvation of connection.'
Amit turns around the old joke 'I read Playboy for the stories': 'No, the thing is I actually did.'

Editor Nomsita was browsing a long Playboy article on psychedelic drugs, and Ajay asks if she's underage for them. Amit: 'Nobody nobody is underage for psychedelic drugs. So I've never had any. I'm just saying random things.'
Ajay on first meeting Playboys in his IIT hostel: 'I mean in the wing it was common property.'
Amit's twelve-year-old novel 'Tales of Saint Johns' opened with chapter one, 'Tantalising Tantrums', 'which at least alliterates.'
Ajay rounds off Amit's diary story with 'In what furnace was thy brain?', a line from William Blake's 'The Tyger'.
Ajay admits he never read Biggles. Amit: 'Shocking. Your education is incomplete.'

The shared childhood reading of their generation: Enid Blyton (The Mystery of Banshee Towers, the Five Find-Outers, the Secret Seven), the Hardy Boys by 'Franklin W. Dixon', which Amit recalls was a syndicate of writers, Biggles, and Alfred Hitchcock and the Three Investigators. On screen there was Alfred Hitchcock Presents, a Televista TV on four legs, Doordarshan as the only channel, and weekly Chitrahaar.

Amit once filmed himself shirtless on a camcorder in the late 80s to remember how thin he was. He has the tape but no VHS player, and says he won't trust anyone with that 'precious footage. So it will remain lost forever.'
Ajay on Amit's habit of buying Filofaxes he never used: 'Gentle reader, he was thinking about productivity all along.' Amit: 'I'm failing at productivity all along.'
Ajay explains the AWK-to-LaTeX recipe book he and Susan built as PhD students. Amit responds with a mock-reverent 'sashtang pranam' (a full bow).
Amit's MTV visiting cards read 'Creative Animal' and, after a promotion, 'Manic Beast'.
At the college STD booths, a new boy from UP opened his call with a formal 'Pranam, Mataji' (respectful greetings, Mother), and 'everybody's just looking at him saying, What the fuck happened?'

Ajay says rotary dialling meant you knew many numbers by heart. Amit: 'Good answer, but not the full answer.' Friends whose numbers had zeros, the most tiring digit to dial, mattered less once push-buttons arrived.

Ajay on Calcutta: 'there is India and then there is Calcutta, right? I mean everything is worse in Calcutta. What Bengal thinks today the rest of India hopes will never happen to them.' It inverts the old saying about Bengal thinking today what India thinks tomorrow. Amit: 'Only in Calcutta.'
Amit invokes Borges on Ajay's search for a perfect wall map of the Himalayas: 'the only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas. So where are you gonna get that?'

Amit on The Replacements: 'who had the best album called Let It Be. The Beatles are in second place.' And on the song Answering Machine: the line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?' would be lost on a generation asking 'What the fuck is an answering machine, dude?'
Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', which Amit cites to argue that writing shapes the writer.
The Playboy segment also notes that in the 1980s the two prestige venues for short fiction were The New Yorker and Playboy, and that India had no Debonair yet in 1967.
